Methods · Part I

Foundations and complex numbers

Units 1–3 · 17 methods

Part I (PDF) All parts

Units 1–3. The first unit’s methods are working tools for the whole course: solving an inequality, finding a domain, inverting a function, solving an equation. Units 2 and 3 carry them into the complex numbers, where most problems begin by choosing a form: Cartesian for sums, polar or exponential for products, powers and roots.

Unit 1 · Foundations: numbers, sets and functions

The notes · The problems · Name the method

Six methods cover the unit’s computations. Its other problems (sums in Σ\SigmaΣ notation, hyperbolic identities, reading a piecewise definition, the irrationality proof) are single moves, done directly as the notes do them.

1.1 Solving an inequality by sign analysis

Problem. Solve an inequality in one real variable, and give the solution set as an interval or a union of intervals.

Method

  1. Bring everything to one side, F(x)>0F(x)>0F(x)>0 (or <<<, ≤\le≤, ≥\ge≥). For a quotient, combine into a single fraction.

  2. Factor the numerator and the denominator into linear factors. A factor with no real zero, such as x2+1x^2+1x2+1, has one sign everywhere: note its sign.

  3. Mark every zero of the numerator and of the denominator on a number line. Between consecutive marked points FFF keeps one sign: find it from a test point, or by counting negative factors. For x−ax−b\tfrac{x-a}{x-b}x−bx−a​ this is the notes’ rule for (x−a)(x−b)(x-a)(x-b)(x−a)(x−b): negative exactly between aaa and bbb, positive outside.

  4. Keep the intervals with the required sign. Include a zero of the numerator only for ≤\le≤ or ≥\ge≥. Never include a zero of the denominator.

  5. Write the answer in interval notation: a square bracket includes the endpoint, a round one excludes it, and ±∞\pm\infty±∞ always takes a round one.

Example Solve 6x≤x−1\dfrac{6}{x}\le x-1x6​≤x−1.

Subtract 6x\tfrac6xx6​ from both sides and combine: x−1−6x=x2−x−6x=(x−3)(x+2)x≥0.x-1-\frac6x=\frac{x^2-x-6}{x}=\frac{(x-3)(x+2)}{x}\ge 0 .x−1−x6​=xx2−x−6​=x(x−3)(x+2)​≥0. Call the left-hand side F(x)F(x)F(x). The numerator is zero at x=−2x=-2x=−2 and x=3x=3x=3, the denominator at x=0x=0x=0, and the signs of the three factors fix the sign of FFF on each interval between them: x+2xx−3F(x)x<−2−−−−−2<x<0+−−+0<x<3++−−x>3++++\begin{array}{c|ccc|c} & x+2 & x & x-3 & F(x) \\ \hline x<-2 & - & - & - & - \\ -2<x<0 & + & - & - & + \\ 0<x<3 & + & + & - & - \\ x>3 & + & + & + & + \end{array}x<−2−2<x<00<x<3x>3​x+2−+++​x−−++​x−3−−−+​F(x)−+−+​​ We need ≥0\ge 0≥0: keep the two positive intervals, include x=−2x=-2x=−2 and x=3x=3x=3 (zeros of the numerator) and exclude x=0x=0x=0:   [−2,0)∪[3,∞)  \boxed{\;[-2,0)\cup[3,\infty)\;}[−2,0)∪[3,∞)​

Check. One test point in each interval, in the original inequality: x=−1x=-1x=−1 gives −6≤−2-6\le-2−6≤−2 and x=4x=4x=4 gives 32≤3\tfrac32\le323​≤3, both true; x=−3x=-3x=−3 gives −2≤−4-2\le-4−2≤−4 and x=1x=1x=1 gives 6≤06\le06≤0, both false. Then the endpoints: at x=−2x=-2x=−2 and x=3x=3x=3 the two sides are equal, so both are included; at x=0x=0x=0 the left side is undefined, so it is excluded.

Variants. A linear inequality is solved directly, reversing the sign whenever you multiply or divide by a negative number. A modulus is removed first, for a>0a>0a>0: ∣x∣≤a  ⟺  −a≤x≤a\left|x\right|\le a\;\Longleftrightarrow\;-a\le x\le a∣x∣≤a⟺−a≤x≤a and ∣x∣≥a  ⟺  x≤−a\left|x\right|\ge a\;\Longleftrightarrow\;x\le -a∣x∣≥a⟺x≤−a or x≥ax\ge ax≥a.

Pitfalls

  • Multiplying both sides by xxx, whose sign you do not know. Above, it gives 6≤x2−x6\le x^2-x6≤x2−x, so x≤−2x\le-2x≤−2 or x≥3x\ge3x≥3: the interval (−2,0)(-2,0)(−2,0) is lost and (−∞,−2)(-\infty,-2)(−∞,−2) wrongly gained.

  • Including a zero of the denominator because the inequality is ≥\ge≥.

  • Writing [3,∞][3,\infty][3,∞]: ∞\infty∞ is not a number, so it cannot be included.

1.2 Maximal domain, and range by building up

Problem. A function is given only by a formula. Find its maximal domain, the largest set of real inputs for which the formula makes sense. Find its range, the set of values it actually takes.

Method

  1. List every restriction the formula imposes: a denominator ≠0\ne0=0; the expression under an even root ≥0\ge0≥0; the expression inside a logarithm >0>0>0; the input of arcsin⁡\arcsinarcsin or arccos⁡\arccosarccos in [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1].

  2. Solve each restriction (an inequality: Method 1.1).

  3. Intersect the solution sets, and write the domain in set-builder notation and as an interval or a union.

  4. For the range, first rewrite the formula so that xxx appears only once, as in x+1x=1+1x\tfrac{x+1}{x}=1+\tfrac1xxx+1​=1+x1​. Start from the innermost piece and the set of values it takes as xxx runs over the domain.

  5. Push that set through each operation in turn: a shift, a stretch, a reciprocal, a root. Each must be increasing or decreasing on the current set, so that endpoints go to endpoints. A decreasing step (a minus sign, a reciprocal of positive numbers) reverses the order of the endpoints.

  6. Say which endpoint values are attained and which are only approached.

Example Find the maximal domain of f(x)=ln⁡(5−x)x+2f(x)=\dfrac{\ln(5-x)}{\sqrt{x+2}}f(x)=x+2​ln(5−x)​, and the range of g(x)=1+4x2+2g(x)=1+\dfrac{4}{x^2+2}g(x)=1+x2+24​.

For fff, the logarithm needs 5−x>05-x>05−x>0, so x<5x<5x<5. The root needs x+2≥0x+2\ge0x+2≥0, and since it is in the denominator it also must not vanish: x+2>0x+2>0x+2>0, so x>−2x>-2x>−2. Intersecting,   { x∈R  :  −2<x<5 }=(−2,5)  \boxed{\;\left\{\,x\in\mathbb{R} \;:\; -2<x<5\,\right\}=(-2,5)\;}{x∈R:−2<x<5}=(−2,5)​ For ggg the domain is R\mathbb{R}R. Build up from the inside: x2∈[0,∞)  ⟹  x2+2∈[2,∞)  ⟹  4x2+2∈(0,2]  ⟹  g(x)∈(1,3].x^2\in[0,\infty)\;\Longrightarrow\; x^2+2\in[2,\infty) \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{4}{x^2+2}\in(0,2] \;\Longrightarrow\; g(x)\in(1,3].x2∈[0,∞)⟹x2+2∈[2,∞)⟹x2+24​∈(0,2]⟹g(x)∈(1,3]. The reciprocal reverses the order: the smallest denominator, 222, gives the largest value, 222. The value 333 is attained at x=0x=0x=0; the value 111 is approached as ∣x∣→∞\left|x\right|\to\infty∣x∣→∞ but never reached. The range is (1,3]\boxed{(1,3]}(1,3]​.

Check. Test a value just outside each claimed endpoint: f(−2)f(-2)f(−2) divides by zero and f(5)f(5)f(5) takes ln⁡0\ln 0ln0; g(x)=1g(x)=1g(x)=1 would need 4x2+2=0\tfrac4{x^2+2}=0x2+24​=0, which has no solution, and g(x)>3g(x)>3g(x)>3 would need x2+2<2x^2+2<2x2+2<2, which has none either.

Pitfalls

  • An even root in a denominator needs the expression under it strictly positive, not just non-negative.

  • Simplifying before reading off the domain: x2−1x−1\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}x−1x2−1​ simplifies to x+1x+1x+1, but x=1x=1x=1 is still excluded.

  • Giving the codomain as the range. The range is what is attained.

1.3 Composition, decomposition and the inverse function

Problem. Form a composite f∘gf\circ gf∘g with its domain; write a given function as a composite of simpler ones; find the inverse of a function, with its domain.

Method

  1. Composite: (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x))(f\circ g)(x)=f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)(f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)). Substitute g(x)g(x)g(x) for the variable of fff.

  2. Its domain: the xxx in the domain of ggg for which g(x)g(x)g(x) lies in the domain of fff. Decide it before simplifying the formula.

  3. Decomposition: name the outer function F(u)F(u)F(u), the last operation applied, with a fresh letter uuu, and the inner function G(x)G(x)G(x), the whole expression it is applied to.

  4. Inverse: show fff is injective, usually by showing it is strictly monotonic on its domain, and find its range.

  5. Write y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x) and solve for xxx in terms of yyy.

  6. Rename the variable to write f−1(x)f^{-1}(x)f−1(x). The domain of f−1f^{-1}f−1 is the range of fff, and its range is the domain of fff.

Example Let f(x)=xf(x)=\sqrt xf(x)=x​ and g(x)=4−xg(x)=4-xg(x)=4−x. Find f∘gf\circ gf∘g and g∘fg\circ fg∘f with their domains, and the inverse of h=g∘fh=g\circ fh=g∘f. Then decompose p(x)=e−x2/2p(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-x^2/2}p(x)=e−x2/2.

(f∘g)(x)=4−x(f\circ g)(x)=\sqrt{4-x}(f∘g)(x)=4−x​, defined when 4−x≥04-x\ge04−x≥0: domain (−∞,4](-\infty,4](−∞,4]. And (g∘f)(x)=4−x(g\circ f)(x)=4-\sqrt x(g∘f)(x)=4−x​, defined when xxx is in the domain of fff: domain [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞).

h(x)=4−xh(x)=4-\sqrt xh(x)=4−x​ is strictly decreasing on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞), since x\sqrt xx​ is strictly increasing. Its range is (−∞,4](-\infty,4](−∞,4], with 444 attained at x=0x=0x=0. Solve y=4−xy=4-\sqrt xy=4−x​: x=4−y\sqrt x=4-yx​=4−y, so x=(4−y)2x=(4-y)^2x=(4−y)2. Hence   h−1(x)=(4−x)2  \boxed{\;h^{-1}(x)=(4-x)^2\;}h−1(x)=(4−x)2​ with domain (−∞,4](-\infty,4](−∞,4], the range of hhh, and range [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞), the domain of hhh. For ppp, the last operation is raising e\mathrm{e}e to a power, applied to −x2/2-x^2/2−x2/2: G(x)=−12x2G(x)=-\tfrac12x^2G(x)=−21​x2 and F(u)=euF(u)=\mathrm{e}^uF(u)=eu, so p=F∘Gp=F\circ Gp=F∘G.

Check. h(h−1(1))=4−9=1h\bigl(h^{-1}(1)\bigr)=4-\sqrt{9}=1h(h−1(1))=4−9​=1 and h−1(h(9))=h−1(1)=9h^{-1}\bigl(h(9)\bigr)=h^{-1}(1)=9h−1(h(9))=h−1(1)=9.

Pitfalls

  • Reading the domain off the simplified formula. With g(x)=xg(x)=\sqrt xg(x)=x​ and f(x)=x2f(x)=x^2f(x)=x2, (f∘g)(x)=x(f\circ g)(x)=x(f∘g)(x)=x, but only for x≥0x\ge0x≥0.

  • Dropping the domain of the inverse. (4−x)2(4-x)^2(4−x)2 on all of R\mathbb{R}R is not injective; it inverts hhh only on (−∞,4](-\infty,4](−∞,4].

1.4 Testing a property: injective, surjective, even, odd, periodic

Problem. Decide whether f ⁣:A→Bf\colon A\to Bf:A→B is injective, surjective or bijective; whether it is even, odd or neither; and find its period.

Method

  1. Injective: show that fff is strictly monotonic on AAA, or that f(x1)=f(x2)f(x_1)=f(x_2)f(x1​)=f(x2​) forces x1=x2x_1=x_2x1​=x2​. To refute it, give x1≠x2x_1\ne x_2x1​=x2​ with f(x1)=f(x2)f(x_1)=f(x_2)f(x1​)=f(x2​).

  2. Surjective: solve y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x) for x∈Ax\in Ax∈A, for every y∈By\in By∈B; equivalently, show that the range is all of BBB. To refute it, give one y∈By\in By∈B that is never attained.

  3. Even or odd: check that the domain is symmetric about 000. Compute f(−x)f(-x)f(−x), simplify, and compare it with f(x)f(x)f(x) and with −f(x)-f(x)−f(x).

  4. Neither: give one xxx with f(−x)≠f(x)f(-x)\ne f(x)f(−x)=f(x) and one with f(−x)≠−f(x)f(-x)\ne -f(x)f(−x)=−f(x). A single xxx can do both.

  5. Period: for a non-constant fff, find the smallest T>0T>0T>0 with f(x+T)=f(x)f(x+T)=f(x)f(x+T)=f(x) for all xxx, if there is one. If fff has period TTT, then f(bx)f(bx)f(bx) has period T/bT/bT/b for b>0b>0b>0.

Example Let f ⁣:R→Rf\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}f:R→R, f(x)=x1+x2f(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}f(x)=1+x2x​. Is it even or odd, injective, surjective? And what is the period of q(x)=cos⁡πx2q(x)=\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{2}q(x)=cos2πx​?

f(−x)=−x1+x2=−f(x)f(-x)=\dfrac{-x}{1+x^2}=-f(x)f(−x)=1+x2−x​=−f(x) on the symmetric domain R\mathbb{R}R, so fff is odd.

Solve y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x) for xxx: yx2−x+y=0yx^2-x+y=0yx2−x+y=0. For y≠0y\ne0y=0 this quadratic has discriminant 1−4y21-4y^21−4y2, so it has a real root only when ∣y∣≤12\left|y\right|\le\tfrac12∣y∣≤21​ (and y=0y=0y=0 gives x=0x=0x=0). The range is [−12,12][-\tfrac12,\tfrac12][−21​,21​], so y=1y=1y=1 is never attained: fff is not surjective.

For 0<∣y∣<120<\left|y\right|<\tfrac120<∣y∣<21​ there are two roots. Taking y=25y=\tfrac25y=52​ gives 2x2−5x+2=02x^2-5x+2=02x2−5x+2=0, so x=2x=2x=2 or x=12x=\tfrac12x=21​: f(2)=25=f(12)f(2)=\tfrac25=f(\tfrac12)f(2)=52​=f(21​), and fff is not injective.

cos⁡\coscos has period 2π2\pi2π, so qqq has period 2π/π2=42\pi\big/\tfrac{\pi}{2}=\boxed{4}2π/2π​=4​.

Check. q(x+4)=cos⁡(πx2+2π)=q(x)q(x+4)=\cos\bigl(\tfrac{\pi x}{2}+2\pi\bigr)=q(x)q(x+4)=cos(2πx​+2π)=q(x), and no smaller TTT works: q(T)=q(0)=1q(T)=q(0)=1q(T)=q(0)=1 needs πT2\tfrac{\pi T}{2}2πT​ to be a multiple of 2π2\pi2π, so TTT is a multiple of 444. And f(±1)=±12f(\pm1)=\pm\tfrac12f(±1)=±21​, the ends of the range, are attained.

Pitfalls

  • Judging on the wrong domain or codomain. The verdict belongs to the rule together with AAA and BBB: x2x^2x2 is bijective as a map [0,∞)→[0,∞)[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)[0,∞)→[0,∞).

  • Proving evenness from one value. f(−x)=f(x)f(-x)=f(x)f(−x)=f(x) must hold for every xxx; a single value can only refute it.

  • Calling a function even or odd when its domain is not symmetric: x\sqrt xx​ is neither.

1.5 Transforming a graph from a base graph

Problem. Sketch y=a f(b(x−c))+dy=a\,f\bigl(b(x-c)\bigr)+dy=af(b(x−c))+d from a graph you know, or name the transformations that produce a given formula.

Method

  1. Write the target in the form a f(b(x−c))+da\,f\bigl(b(x-c)\bigr)+daf(b(x−c))+d: complete the square, or factor the coefficient of xxx out of the bracket.

  2. Every point (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) of y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x) moves to (c+ub, d+av)\bigl(c+\tfrac{u}{b},\ d+a v\bigr)(c+bu​, d+av). Horizontally: scale by 1b\tfrac1bb1​ (reflecting if b<0b<0b<0), then shift by ccc. Vertically: scale by aaa (reflecting if a<0a<0a<0), then shift by ddd.

  3. Move the key points and the asymptotes by that rule. A moved intercept need not be an intercept of the new graph: find those from its formula, with x=0x=0x=0 and y=0y=0y=0.

  4. Read off what is asked: the domain, the range, where the function increases.

  5. Sketch, labelling the points you moved.

Example Obtain y=1+4−2xy=1+\sqrt{4-2x}y=1+4−2x​ from y=xy=\sqrt xy=x​, and give its domain and range.

Factor the coefficient of xxx out of the bracket: 4−2x=−2(x−2)4-2x=-2(x-2)4−2x=−2(x−2), so the target is f(b(x−c))+df\bigl(b(x-c)\bigr)+df(b(x−c))+d with f= f=\sqrt{\ }f= ​, a=1a=1a=1, b=−2b=-2b=−2, c=2c=2c=2, d=1d=1d=1. The graph is compressed horizontally by 12\tfrac1221​ and reflected in the yyy-axis, then shifted 222 right and 111 up. The point (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) goes to (2−u2, 1+v)\bigl(2-\tfrac u2,\ 1+v\bigr)(2−2u​, 1+v): (0,0)↦(2,1),(4,2)↦(0,3),(16,4)↦(−6,5).(0,0)\mapsto(2,1),\qquad\allowbreak (4,2)\mapsto(0,3),\qquad\allowbreak (16,4)\mapsto(-6,5).(0,0)↦(2,1),(4,2)↦(0,3),(16,4)↦(−6,5). The graph starts at (2,1)(2,1)(2,1) and rises to the left, so   domain (−∞,2],range [1,∞)  \boxed{\;\text{domain }(-\infty,2],\quad \text{range }[1,\infty)\;}domain (−∞,2],range [1,∞)​ and the function is decreasing. It meets the yyy-axis at (0,3)(0,3)(0,3) and never meets the xxx-axis, since y≥1y\ge1y≥1.

Check. Substitute the moved points: 1+4−0=31+\sqrt{4-0}=31+4−0​=3 and 1+4+12=51+\sqrt{4+12}=51+4+12​=5. The domain also follows from 4−2x≥04-2x\ge04−2x≥0.

Pitfalls

  • Reading f(2x−4)f(2x-4)f(2x−4) as a shift by 444. Factor first: f(2(x−2))f\bigl(2(x-2)\bigr)f(2(x−2)) is a shift by 222.

  • Moving the wrong way: f(x−c)f(x-c)f(x−c) moves the graph right by ccc when c>0c>0c>0.

  • Doing the vertical steps in the wrong order: af(x)+da f(x)+daf(x)+d scales first, then shifts; a(f(x)+d)a\bigl(f(x)+d\bigr)a(f(x)+d) is a different graph.

1.6 Exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric equations

Problem. Solve an equation in which the unknown sits inside an exponential, a logarithm or a trigonometric function.

Method

  1. If a logarithm of an expression in xxx appears, find where it is defined first.

  2. Use the index and log laws to reduce the equation to one exponential or one logarithm on each side, or substitute u=exu=\mathrm{e}^xu=ex (so u>0u>0u>0) to get a polynomial in uuu.

  3. Take ln⁡\lnln of both sides, or make each side a power of e\mathrm{e}e, and solve. After a substitution, solve the polynomial for uuu, keep only the roots with u>0u>0u>0, and set x=ln⁡ux=\ln ux=lnu.

  4. Reject any value outside the domain from step 1.

  5. For a trigonometric equation, isolate sin⁡θ=c\sin\theta=csinθ=c, cos⁡θ=c\cos\theta=ccosθ=c or tan⁡θ=c\tan\theta=ctanθ=c, where θ\thetaθ is the whole argument (such as 2x2x2x), factoring first if there are several terms.

  6. Take the principal value α\alphaα from the table or the inverse function. The second value in one period comes from the symmetry: π−α\pi-\alphaπ−α for sine, −α-\alpha−α for cosine; tangent has only one value per period.

  7. Add whole periods to θ\thetaθ (2π2\pi2π for sine and cosine, π\piπ for tangent), then solve for xxx, and list every solution in the interval asked for.

Example Solve (a) ln⁡(x+4)=2ln⁡x\ln(x+4)=2\ln xln(x+4)=2lnx, and (b) 2sin⁡2x=sin⁡x2\sin^2x=\sin x2sin2x=sinx on [0,2π)[0,2\pi)[0,2π).

(a) Both logarithms need x>0x>0x>0 (then x+4>0x+4>0x+4>0 too). By the power law 2ln⁡x=ln⁡(x2)2\ln x=\ln(x^2)2lnx=ln(x2), so ln⁡(x+4)=ln⁡(x2)\ln(x+4)=\ln(x^2)ln(x+4)=ln(x2), x+4=x2x+4=x^2x+4=x2 and x2−x−4=0x^2-x-4=0x2−x−4=0, with roots x=1±172x=\tfrac{1\pm\sqrt{17}}{2}x=21±17​​. Only the plus sign gives x>0x>0x>0: x=1+172\boxed{x=\tfrac{1+\sqrt{17}}{2}}x=21+17​​​.

(b) Bring everything to one side and factor: sin⁡x (2sin⁡x−1)=0\sin x\,(2\sin x-1)=0sinx(2sinx−1)=0. Then sin⁡x=0\sin x=0sinx=0 gives x=0, πx=0,\ \pix=0, π. And sin⁡x=12\sin x=\tfrac12sinx=21​ gives the principal value π6\tfrac\pi66π​ and the second value π−π6=5π6\pi-\tfrac\pi6=\tfrac{5\pi}6π−6π​=65π​. So   x∈{0, π6, 5π6, π}  \boxed{\;x\in\Bigl\{0,\ \tfrac\pi6,\ \tfrac{5\pi}6,\ \pi\Bigr\}\;}x∈{0, 6π​, 65π​, π}​

Check. Substitute: in (a), x2=9+172=x+4x^2=\tfrac{9+\sqrt{17}}{2}=x+4x2=29+17​​=x+4 and x>0x>0x>0; in (b), 2sin⁡2x=sin⁡x2\sin^2x=\sin x2sin2x=sinx holds at each of the four values (12=12\tfrac12=\tfrac1221​=21​ at π6\tfrac\pi66π​ and 5π6\tfrac{5\pi}665π​). Then count: each factor, sin⁡x=0\sin x=0sinx=0 and sin⁡x=12\sin x=\tfrac12sinx=21​, has two solutions in [0,2π)[0,2\pi)[0,2π), so there are four.

Pitfalls

  • Dividing by sin⁡x\sin xsinx: it loses the solutions x=0x=0x=0 and x=πx=\pix=π. Factor instead, or check the zeros of what you divide by.

  • Keeping x=1−172x=\tfrac{1-\sqrt{17}}{2}x=21−17​​ in (a). It satisfies ln⁡(x+4)=ln⁡(x2)\ln(x+4)=\ln(x^2)ln(x+4)=ln(x2), but ln⁡x\ln xlnx is not defined there: 2ln⁡x=ln⁡(x2)2\ln x=\ln(x^2)2lnx=ln(x2) holds only for x>0x>0x>0.

  • Stopping at the principal value. arcsin⁡12\arcsin\tfrac12arcsin21​ is one number; the equation sin⁡x=12\sin x=\tfrac12sinx=21​ has two solutions in every period.

Unit 2 · Complex numbers I: algebra and geometry

The notes · The problems · Name the method

Six methods. The powers of i\mathrm{i}i are a step inside the first, and the short proofs of the conjugate and modulus rules are the last step of Method 2.5.

2.1 Cartesian arithmetic, and division by the conjugate

Problem. Write a sum, product, power or quotient of complex numbers in the form a+b ia+b\,\mathrm{i}a+bi; find a conjugate or a modulus.

Method

  1. Sum or difference: real parts with real parts, imaginary parts with imaginary parts.

  2. Product: expand the brackets, replace i2\mathrm{i}^2i2 by −1-1−1, and group into (… )+(… ) i(\dots)+(\dots)\,\mathrm{i}(…)+(…)i. For in\mathrm{i}^nin, divide nnn by 444: in=ir\mathrm{i}^n=\mathrm{i}^rin=ir, where rrr is the remainder, read from 1, i, −1, −i1,\ \mathrm{i},\ -1,\ -\mathrm{i}1, i, −1, −i. For n<0n<0n<0, first add a multiple of 444: i−5=i−5+8=i3=−i\mathrm{i}^{-5}=\mathrm{i}^{-5+8}=\mathrm{i}^3=-\mathrm{i}i−5=i−5+8=i3=−i.

  3. Quotient: multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate c−d ic-d\,\mathrm{i}c−di of the denominator c+d ic+d\,\mathrm{i}c+di. The denominator becomes the real number c2+d2c^2+d^2c2+d2.

  4. Expand the numerator, replace i2\mathrm{i}^2i2 by −1-1−1, and split into pc2+d2+qc2+d2 i\dfrac{p}{c^2+d^2}+\dfrac{q}{c^2+d^2}\,\mathrm{i}c2+d2p​+c2+d2q​i.

  5. Conjugate: flip the sign of the imaginary part. Modulus: ∣a+b i∣=a2+b2\left|a+b\,\mathrm{i}\right|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}∣a+bi∣=a2+b2​, and zz‾=∣z∣2z\overline{z}=\left|z\right|^2zz=∣z∣2.

Example Write 7+i1−2i−i23\dfrac{7+\mathrm{i}}{1-2\mathrm{i}}-\mathrm{i}^{23}1−2i7+i​−i23 in the form a+b ia+b\,\mathrm{i}a+bi, and find its modulus.

Multiply the top and the bottom by 1+2i1+2\mathrm{i}1+2i, the conjugate of the denominator: 7+i1−2i=(7+i)(1+2i)(1−2i)(1+2i)=7+14i+i+2i212+22=5+15i5=1+3i.\frac{7+\mathrm{i}}{1-2\mathrm{i}}=\frac{(7+\mathrm{i})(1+2\mathrm{i})}{(1-2\mathrm{i})(1+2\mathrm{i})} =\frac{7+14\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{i}+2\mathrm{i}^2}{1^2+2^2}=\frac{5+15\mathrm{i}}{5}=1+3\mathrm{i}.1−2i7+i​=(1−2i)(1+2i)(7+i)(1+2i)​=12+227+14i+i+2i2​=55+15i​=1+3i. Since 23=4⋅5+323=4\cdot5+323=4⋅5+3, i23=i3=−i\mathrm{i}^{23}=\mathrm{i}^3=-\mathrm{i}i23=i3=−i. So the number is 1+3i−(−i)=1+4i1+3\mathrm{i}-(-\mathrm{i})=\boxed{1+4\mathrm{i}}1+3i−(−i)=1+4i​, with modulus 12+42=17\sqrt{1^2+4^2}=\boxed{\sqrt{17}}12+42​=17​​.

Check. Multiply the quotient back by the denominator: (1+3i)(1−2i)=1−2i+3i−6i2=7+i(1+3\mathrm{i})(1-2\mathrm{i})=1-2\mathrm{i}+3\mathrm{i}-6\mathrm{i}^2=7+\mathrm{i}(1+3i)(1−2i)=1−2i+3i−6i2=7+i. Then i23=−i\mathrm{i}^{23}=-\mathrm{i}i23=−i because (−i) i=1=i24(-\mathrm{i})\,\mathrm{i}=1=\mathrm{i}^{24}(−i)i=1=i24, and (1+4i)(1−4i)=1−16i2=17=∣1+4i∣2(1+4\mathrm{i})(1-4\mathrm{i})=1-16\mathrm{i}^2=17=\left|1+4\mathrm{i}\right|^2(1+4i)(1−4i)=1−16i2=17=∣1+4i∣2.

Pitfalls

  • Dividing part by part: a+bic+di≠ac+bd i\dfrac{a+b\mathrm{i}}{c+d\mathrm{i}}\ne\dfrac ac+\dfrac bd\,\mathrm{i}c+dia+bi​=ca​+db​i.

  • Losing the sign of i2\mathrm{i}^2i2: 2i⋅i=−22\mathrm{i}\cdot\mathrm{i}=-22i⋅i=−2, not 222.

  • Putting i\mathrm{i}i inside the modulus: ∣1+4i∣=1+16\left|1+4\mathrm{i}\right|=\sqrt{1+16}∣1+4i∣=1+16​, not 1+(4i)2\sqrt{1+(4\mathrm{i})^2}1+(4i)2​.

2.2 Real polynomials: complex roots in conjugate pairs

Problem. Solve a real quadratic with a negative discriminant; given one non-real root of a real cubic or quartic, find all its roots.

Method

  1. Quadratic: complete the square to (x+p)2+q=0(x+p)^2+q=0(x+p)2+q=0 with q>0q>0q>0. Then (x+p)2=−q=(iq)2(x+p)^2=-q=(\mathrm{i}\sqrt q)^2(x+p)2=−q=(iq​)2, so x=−p±iqx=-p\pm\mathrm{i}\sqrt qx=−p±iq​. Or use the formula: D=b2−4ac<0D=b^2-4ac<0D=b2−4ac<0 and x=−b±i4ac−b22ax=\dfrac{-b\pm\mathrm{i}\sqrt{4ac-b^2}}{2a}x=2a−b±i4ac−b2​​.

  2. A polynomial with real coefficients and a root α\alphaα also has the root α‾\overline{\alpha}α.

  3. Multiply the pair into a real quadratic: (x−α)(x−α‾)=x2−2Re(α) x+∣α∣2(x-\alpha)(x-\overline{\alpha})=x^2-2\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}(\alpha)\,x+\left|\alpha\right|^2(x−α)(x−α)=x2−2Re(α)x+∣α∣2.

  4. Find the other factor by comparing coefficients (or by long division). Its roots (by step 1, if it is a quadratic) are the remaining roots.

  5. List every root.

Example (a) Solve x2−6x+13=0x^2-6x+13=0x2−6x+13=0. (b) Given that −1+2i-1+2\mathrm{i}−1+2i is a root of p(x)=2x3+x2+4x−15p(x)=2x^3+x^2+4x-15p(x)=2x3+x2+4x−15, find the other two.

(a) Complete the square: (x−3)2+4=0(x-3)^2+4=0(x−3)2+4=0, so (x−3)2=−4=(2i)2(x-3)^2=-4=(2\mathrm{i})^2(x−3)2=−4=(2i)2 and x=3±2i\boxed{x=3\pm2\mathrm{i}}x=3±2i​.

(b) The coefficients are real, so −1−2i-1-2\mathrm{i}−1−2i is a root too. The pair gives the real factor x2−2⋅(−1) x+∣−1+2i∣2=x2+2x+5.x^2-2\cdot(-1)\,x+\left|-1+2\mathrm{i}\right|^2=x^2+2x+5 .x2−2⋅(−1)x+∣−1+2i∣2=x2+2x+5. The x3x^3x3 terms need 2x2x2x in the other factor, so write p(x)=(x2+2x+5)(2x+k)p(x)=(x^2+2x+5)(2x+k)p(x)=(x2+2x+5)(2x+k) and compare the constant terms: 5k=−155k=-155k=−15, so k=−3k=-3k=−3. The roots are −1+2i, −1−2i, 32\boxed{-1+2\mathrm{i},\ -1-2\mathrm{i},\ \tfrac32}−1+2i, −1−2i, 23​​.

Check. Expand: (x2+2x+5)(2x−3)=2x3+x2+4x−15(x^2+2x+5)(2x-3)=2x^3+x^2+4x-15(x2+2x+5)(2x−3)=2x3+x2+4x−15. In (a), the pair multiplies back to x2−2⋅3 x+∣3+2i∣2=x2−6x+13x^2-2\cdot3\,x+\left|3+2\mathrm{i}\right|^2=x^2-6x+13x2−2⋅3x+∣3+2i∣2=x2−6x+13.

Pitfalls

  • Dropping the i\mathrm{i}i: from (x−3)2=−4(x-3)^2=-4(x−3)2=−4 it is x−3=±2ix-3=\pm2\mathrm{i}x−3=±2i, because (2i)2=−4(2\mathrm{i})^2=-4(2i)2=−4. Do not write −4\sqrt{-4}−4​.

  • Using the conjugate-pair rule on a polynomial with non-real coefficients: x−ix-\mathrm{i}x−i has the root i\mathrm{i}i but not −i-\mathrm{i}−i.

  • Stopping at the pair: a cubic has a third root, and it is real.

2.3 Cartesian and polar form, with the quadrant rule

Problem. Write a nonzero z=a+b iz=a+b\,\mathrm{i}z=a+bi in polar form r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)r(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)r(cosθ+isinθ) with its principal argument, or convert a polar form back to a+b ia+b\,\mathrm{i}a+bi.

Method

  1. r=∣z∣=a2+b2r=\left|z\right|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}r=∣z∣=a2+b2​.

  2. Sketch the point to see its quadrant. A point on an axis has θ=0, π2, π\theta=0,\ \tfrac\pi2,\ \piθ=0, 2π​, π or −π2-\tfrac\pi2−2π​ directly.

  3. The reference angle is the acute angle α=arctan⁡∣b/a∣\alpha=\arctan\left|b/a\right|α=arctan∣b/a∣.

  4. The principal argument, in (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π], from the quadrant: α\alphaα (first), π−α\pi-\alphaπ−α (second), −π+α-\pi+\alpha−π+α (third), −α-\alpha−α (fourth).

  5. Write z=r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)z=r(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)z=r(cosθ+isinθ).

  6. Back to Cartesian: evaluate cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ and sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ, and multiply by rrr.

Example Write z=−3−3 iz=-3-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i}z=−3−3​i in polar form with its principal argument, and w=5(cos⁡3π4+isin⁡3π4)w=5\bigl(\cos\tfrac{3\pi}{4}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\bigr)w=5(cos43π​+isin43π​) in Cartesian form.

r=9+3=23r=\sqrt{9+3}=2\sqrt3r=9+3​=23​. Both parts are negative: the third quadrant. The reference angle is α=arctan⁡33=π6\alpha=\arctan\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}=\tfrac\pi6α=arctan33​​=6π​, so θ=−π+π6=−5π6\theta=-\pi+\tfrac\pi6=-\tfrac{5\pi}6θ=−π+6π​=−65π​ and   z=23(cos⁡(−5π6)+isin⁡(−5π6))  \boxed{\;z=2\sqrt3\Bigl(\cos\bigl(-\tfrac{5\pi}6\bigr)+\mathrm{i}\sin\bigl(-\tfrac{5\pi}6\bigr)\Bigr)\;}z=23​(cos(−65π​)+isin(−65π​))​ For www: cos⁡3π4=−22\cos\tfrac{3\pi}4=-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2cos43π​=−22​​ and sin⁡3π4=22\sin\tfrac{3\pi}4=\tfrac{\sqrt2}2sin43π​=22​​, so w=−522+522 i\boxed{w=-\tfrac{5\sqrt2}{2}+\tfrac{5\sqrt2}{2}\,\mathrm{i}}w=−252​​+252​​i​.

Check. Convert back: 23(−32−12i)=−3−3 i2\sqrt3\bigl(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2-\tfrac12\mathrm{i}\bigr)=-3-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i}23​(−23​​−21​i)=−3−3​i.

Pitfalls

  • Taking arctan⁡(b/a)\arctan(b/a)arctan(b/a) as the argument. Here it gives arctan⁡33=π6\arctan\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}=\tfrac\pi6arctan33​​=6π​, a first-quadrant angle for a third-quadrant point. The sketch fixes the quadrant, not the tangent.

  • Giving 7π6\tfrac{7\pi}667π​ when the principal argument is asked for. It is an argument of zzz, but not in (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π].

2.4 Multiplying and dividing in polar form; rotation

Problem. Multiply or divide complex numbers given in polar form; rotate and scale a point of the plane.

Method

  1. Write each factor in polar form (Method 2.3).

  2. Product: multiply the moduli and add the arguments. Quotient: divide the moduli and subtract the arguments.

  3. If the principal argument is asked for and the result is outside (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π], add or subtract 2π2\pi2π.

  4. Convert to a+b ia+b\,\mathrm{i}a+bi if asked.

  5. To turn a point zzz through α\alphaα anticlockwise and scale it by k>0k>0k>0, multiply by k(cos⁡α+isin⁡α)k(\cos\alpha+\mathrm{i}\sin\alpha)k(cosα+isinα). A clockwise turn uses −α-\alpha−α.

Example Let z=2(cos⁡(−2π3)+isin⁡(−2π3))z=2\bigl(\cos(-\tfrac{2\pi}3)+\mathrm{i}\sin(-\tfrac{2\pi}3)\bigr)z=2(cos(−32π​)+isin(−32π​)) and w=4(cos⁡π2+isin⁡π2)w=4\bigl(\cos\tfrac\pi2+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac\pi2\bigr)w=4(cos2π​+isin2π​). Find zwzwzw and z/wz/wz/w in Cartesian form. Then turn 2+4i2+4\mathrm{i}2+4i a quarter turn clockwise and halve its distance from 000.

zwzwzw has modulus 888 and argument −2π3+π2=−π6-\tfrac{2\pi}3+\tfrac\pi2=-\tfrac\pi6−32π​+2π​=−6π​, already in (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π]. So zw=8(32−12 i)=43−4i.zw=8\Bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt3}2-\tfrac12\,\mathrm{i}\Bigr)=\boxed{4\sqrt3-4\mathrm{i}}.zw=8(23​​−21​i)=43​−4i​. z/wz/wz/w has modulus 12\tfrac1221​ and argument −2π3−π2=−7π6-\tfrac{2\pi}3-\tfrac\pi2=-\tfrac{7\pi}6−32π​−2π​=−67π​, which is outside (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π]; add 2π2\pi2π to get 5π6\tfrac{5\pi}665π​: z/w=12(−32+12i)=−34+14 iz/w=\tfrac12\bigl(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2+\tfrac12\mathrm{i}\bigr)=\boxed{-\tfrac{\sqrt3}4+\tfrac14\,\mathrm{i}}z/w=21​(−23​​+21​i)=−43​​+41​i​.

The multiplier has k=12k=\tfrac12k=21​ and α=−π2\alpha=-\tfrac\pi2α=−2π​, so it is 12(cos⁡(−π2)+isin⁡(−π2))=−12i\tfrac12(\cos(-\tfrac\pi2)+\mathrm{i}\sin(-\tfrac\pi2))=-\tfrac12\mathrm{i}21​(cos(−2π​)+isin(−2π​))=−21​i. Then (2+4i)(−12i)=−i−2i2=2−i(2+4\mathrm{i})(-\tfrac12\mathrm{i})=-\mathrm{i}-2\mathrm{i}^2=\boxed{2-\mathrm{i}}(2+4i)(−21​i)=−i−2i2=2−i​.

Check. Undo the turn and the scaling, multiplying by 2i2\mathrm{i}2i: (2−i)⋅2i=4i−2i2=2+4i(2-\mathrm{i})\cdot2\mathrm{i}=4\mathrm{i}-2\mathrm{i}^2=2+4\mathrm{i}(2−i)⋅2i=4i−2i2=2+4i. And zwzwzw is 2⋅4=82\cdot4=82⋅4=8 from 000: 48+16=8\sqrt{48+16}=848+16​=8.

Pitfalls

  • Adding the moduli. They multiply; only the arguments add.

  • Leaving −7π6-\tfrac{7\pi}6−67π​ as the principal argument.

  • Turning the wrong way: cos⁡α+isin⁡α\cos\alpha+\mathrm{i}\sin\alphacosα+isinα with α>0\alpha>0α>0 turns anticlockwise.

2.5 Equating real and imaginary parts

Problem. Find an unknown complex number from an equation it satisfies; prove an identity that holds for all complex numbers.

Method

  1. Write the unknown as z=x+y iz=x+y\,\mathrm{i}z=x+yi with xxx and yyy real (and z‾=x−y i\overline{z}=x-y\,\mathrm{i}z=x−yi).

  2. Expand both sides into (real) + \,+\,+(real) i\,\mathrm{i}i.

  3. Two complex numbers are equal exactly when their real parts are equal and their imaginary parts are equal. That gives two real equations.

  4. Solve the two equations for xxx and yyy.

  5. For an identity in zzz and www, write z=a+b iz=a+b\,\mathrm{i}z=a+bi and w=c+d iw=c+d\,\mathrm{i}w=c+di, expand both sides and compare the parts. Where moduli appear, it is often shorter to use ∣u∣2=u u‾\left|u\right|^2=u\,\overline{u}∣u∣2=uu with the conjugate rules z±w‾=z‾±w‾\overline{z\pm w}=\overline{z}\pm\overline{w}z±w​=z±w and zw‾=z‾ w‾\overline{zw}=\overline{z}\,\overline{w}zw=zw.

Example Find every zzz with 2z+iz‾=3+6i2z+\mathrm{i}\overline{z}=3+6\mathrm{i}2z+iz=3+6i.

Put z=x+y iz=x+y\,\mathrm{i}z=x+yi, so z‾=x−y i\overline{z}=x-y\,\mathrm{i}z=x−yi, and expand: 2x+2y i+i(x−y i)=(2x+y)+(x+2y) i.2x+2y\,\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{i}(x-y\,\mathrm{i})=(2x+y)+(x+2y)\,\mathrm{i}.2x+2yi+i(x−yi)=(2x+y)+(x+2y)i. Equate the parts with those of 3+6i3+6\mathrm{i}3+6i: 2x+y=32x+y=32x+y=3 and x+2y=6x+2y=6x+2y=6. The first gives y=3−2xy=3-2xy=3−2x; then x+6−4x=6x+6-4x=6x+6−4x=6, so x=0x=0x=0 and y=3y=3y=3. The only solution is z=3i\boxed{z=3\mathrm{i}}z=3i​.

Check. Substitute: 2(3i)+i(−3i)=6i+32(3\mathrm{i})+\mathrm{i}(-3\mathrm{i})=6\mathrm{i}+32(3i)+i(−3i)=6i+3.

Pitfalls

  • Treating z‾\overline{z}z as zzz: they have the same real part and opposite imaginary parts.

  • Forgetting that xxx and yyy must be real. If the two equations have no real solution, no zzz satisfies the equation.

  • Checking an identity at one value of zzz. That can refute it but not prove it.

2.6 Reading a locus on the Argand plane

Problem. Describe and sketch a set of points zzz given by distances: a circle ∣z−c∣=r\left|z-c\right|=r∣z−c∣=r, a disc such as ∣z−c∣<r\left|z-c\right|<r∣z−c∣<r, or a line ∣z−a∣=∣z−b∣\left|z-a\right|=\left|z-b\right|∣z−a∣=∣z−b∣.

Method

  1. Read ∣z−c∣\left|z-c\right|∣z−c∣ as the distance from zzz to the point ccc. Rewrite ∣z+c∣\left|z+c\right|∣z+c∣ as ∣z−(−c)∣\left|z-(-c)\right|∣z−(−c)∣ first.

  2. Name the set. ∣z−c∣=r\left|z-c\right|=r∣z−c∣=r is the circle with centre ccc and radius rrr; ∣z−c∣<r\left|z-c\right|<r∣z−c∣<r is the inside of that circle. ∣z−a∣=∣z−b∣\left|z-a\right|=\left|z-b\right|∣z−a∣=∣z−b∣ is the perpendicular bisector of the segment from aaa to bbb.

  3. If you are unsure, put z=x+y iz=x+y\,\mathrm{i}z=x+yi, square both sides, and simplify to an equation (or inequality) in xxx and yyy.

  4. Sketch it. For a circle, mark the centre and the radius; for a bisector, the two points. A boundary that belongs to the set is drawn solid; one that does not (a strict inequality) is drawn dashed.

Example Describe (a) ∣z−1+2i∣=3\left|z-1+2\mathrm{i}\right|=3∣z−1+2i∣=3 and (b) ∣z+2i∣=∣z−4∣\left|z+2\mathrm{i}\right|=\left|z-4\right|∣z+2i∣=∣z−4∣.

(a) ∣z−(1−2i)∣=3\left|z-(1-2\mathrm{i})\right|=3∣z−(1−2i)∣=3: the points at distance 333 from 1−2i1-2\mathrm{i}1−2i, that is, the circle   centre (1,−2), radius 3  \boxed{\;\text{centre }(1,-2),\ \text{radius }3\;}centre (1,−2), radius 3​

(b) ∣z−(−2i)∣=∣z−4∣\left|z-(-2\mathrm{i})\right|=\left|z-4\right|∣z−(−2i)∣=∣z−4∣: the points as far from −2i-2\mathrm{i}−2i as from 444, that is, the perpendicular bisector of the segment from (0,−2)(0,-2)(0,−2) to (4,0)(4,0)(4,0). With z=x+y iz=x+y\,\mathrm{i}z=x+yi and both sides squared, x2+(y+2)2=(x−4)2+y2  ⟺  4y+4=−8x+16  ⟺  y=3−2x.x^2+(y+2)^2=(x-4)^2+y^2 \;\Longleftrightarrow\;4y+4=-8x+16 \;\Longleftrightarrow\;\boxed{y=3-2x}.x2+(y+2)2=(x−4)2+y2⟺4y+4=−8x+16⟺y=3−2x​.

Check. The midpoint (2,−1)(2,-1)(2,−1) of the segment lies on y=3−2xy=3-2xy=3−2x, and the slope −2-2−2 is perpendicular to the segment’s slope 12\tfrac1221​.

Pitfalls

  • Reading ∣z+2i∣\left|z+2\mathrm{i}\right|∣z+2i∣ as the distance from 2i2\mathrm{i}2i. It is the distance from −2i-2\mathrm{i}−2i.

  • Getting the centre’s sign wrong: ∣z−1+2i∣\left|z-1+2\mathrm{i}\right|∣z−1+2i∣ is centred at 1−2i1-2\mathrm{i}1−2i, not at 1+2i1+2\mathrm{i}1+2i.

  • Drawing the boundary of ∣z−c∣<r\left|z-c\right|<r∣z−c∣<r solid.

Unit 3 · Complex numbers II: exponential form, De Moivre, roots

The notes · The problems · Name the method

Five methods, and the problems look alike: most start by writing a number as reiθr\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}reiθ. What decides the method is what the question asks for. The fundamental theorem of algebra is a fact to quote; given one non-real root, a real polynomial is factored as in Method 2.2.

Which method?

The question asks for Method
a product, a quotient or a rotation 3.1, exponential form and index laws
an integer power znz^nzn 3.2, De Moivre (not the binomial theorem)
every www with wn=zw^n=zwn=z; the roots of unity 3.3, nnnth roots
a square root of zzz when arg⁡z\arg zargz is not a standard angle 3.3, variant: equate parts
cos⁡nθ\cos n\thetacosnθ or sin⁡nθ\sin n\thetasinnθ in powers of cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ and sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ 3.4, expand (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)n(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^n(cosθ+isinθ)n
cos⁡nθ\cos^n\thetacosnθ or sin⁡nθ\sin^n\thetasinnθ as a sum of multiple angles 3.4, the inverse Euler formulas
cos⁡\coscos, sin⁡\sinsin, cosh⁡\coshcosh or sinh⁡\sinhsinh of an imaginary number 3.4, the inverse Euler formulas at ix\mathrm{i}xix
one sinusoid equal to a sum of sinusoids of one frequency 3.5, phasors

3.1 Exponential form and the index laws

Problem. Write a nonzero complex number as reiθr\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}reiθ or back as a+b ia+b\,\mathrm{i}a+bi; multiply, divide, invert or rotate in exponential form.

Method

  1. To exponential form: find rrr and the argument θ\thetaθ exactly as for the polar form (Method 2.3, quadrant first), and write z=reiθz=r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}z=reiθ.

  2. Back to Cartesian: reiθ=rcos⁡θ+i rsin⁡θr\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=r\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\,r\sin\thetareiθ=rcosθ+irsinθ.

  3. Product and quotient: multiply or divide the moduli, add or subtract the exponents. The reciprocal is 1re−iθ\tfrac1r\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}r1​e−iθ and the conjugate is re−iθr\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}re−iθ.

  4. Rotation: multiplying by eiα\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}eiα turns a point through α\alphaα anticlockwise about 000 (e−iα\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\alpha}e−iα turns it clockwise), and seiαs\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha}seiα also scales it by sss.

  5. If the principal argument is asked for, bring the exponent into (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π] by whole turns.

Example Let z=−2+2iz=-2+2\mathrm{i}z=−2+2i and w=2−2 iw=\sqrt2-\sqrt2\,\mathrm{i}w=2​−2​i. Find zwzwzw and z/wz/wz/w through the exponential form.

zzz is in the second quadrant with ∣z∣=22\left|z\right|=2\sqrt2∣z∣=22​ and reference angle π4\tfrac\pi44π​, so z=22 ei3π/4z=2\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}3\pi/4}z=22​ei3π/4. www is in the fourth with ∣w∣=2\left|w\right|=2∣w∣=2, so w=2e−iπ/4w=2\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi/4}w=2e−iπ/4. Then zw=42 ei(3π/4−π/4)=42 eiπ/2=42 i,zw=2 ei(3π/4+π/4)=2 eiπ=−2.zw=4\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(3\pi/4-\pi/4)}=4\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/2}=\boxed{4\sqrt2\,\mathrm{i}}, \qquad\allowbreak \frac zw=\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(3\pi/4+\pi/4)}=\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}=\boxed{-\sqrt2}.zw=42​ei(3π/4−π/4)=42​eiπ/2=42​i​,wz​=2​ei(3π/4+π/4)=2​eiπ=−2​​.

Check. In Cartesian form, (−2+2i)(2−2i)=−22+22i+22i+22=42 i(-2+2\mathrm{i})(\sqrt2-\sqrt2\mathrm{i})=-2\sqrt2+2\sqrt2\mathrm{i}+2\sqrt2\mathrm{i}+2\sqrt2=4\sqrt2\,\mathrm{i}(−2+2i)(2​−2​i)=−22​+22​i+22​i+22​=42​i, and (−2)(2−2i)=−2+2i=z(-\sqrt2)(\sqrt2-\sqrt2\mathrm{i})=-2+2\mathrm{i}=z(−2​)(2​−2​i)=−2+2i=z.

Pitfalls

  • Subtracting the exponents the wrong way round in a quotient: it is the argument of the top minus the argument of the bottom.

  • Writing eiθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ with θ\thetaθ in degrees. The exponent is in radians.

  • Taking the argument from arctan⁡(b/a)\arctan(b/a)arctan(b/a) without the quadrant, as in Method 2.3.

3.2 Integer powers by De Moivre

Problem. Compute znz^nzn for an integer nnn, positive or negative.

Method

  1. Write z=reiθz=r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}z=reiθ (Method 3.1).

  2. Then zn=rneinθz^n=r^n\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}n\theta}zn=rneinθ: raise the modulus to the power and multiply the argument by nnn. This works for negative nnn too.

  3. Remove whole turns (2π2\pi2π each) from nθn\thetanθ to bring it into (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π].

  4. Evaluate cos⁡\coscos and sin⁡\sinsin of it and write a+b ia+b\,\mathrm{i}a+bi.

Why it works. De Moivre’s theorem, (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)n=cos⁡nθ+isin⁡nθ(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^n=\cos n\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin n\theta(cosθ+isinθ)n=cosnθ+isinnθ. The proof is by induction: check n=1n=1n=1; assume it for n=kn=kn=k; split (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)k+1(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{k+1}(cosθ+isinθ)k+1 into the kkkth power times one more factor, use the assumption, and add the arguments.

Example Compute (a) (−3−i)7(-\sqrt3-\mathrm{i})^{7}(−3​−i)7 and (b) (1−3 i)−5(1-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i})^{-5}(1−3​i)−5.

(a) −3−i-\sqrt3-\mathrm{i}−3​−i is in the third quadrant with modulus 222 and reference angle π6\tfrac\pi66π​, so −3−i=2e−i5π/6-\sqrt3-\mathrm{i}=2\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}5\pi/6}−3​−i=2e−i5π/6 and (−3−i)7=27e−i35π/6(-\sqrt3-\mathrm{i})^{7}=2^7\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}35\pi/6}(−3​−i)7=27e−i35π/6. Add three whole turns: −35π6+6π=π6-\tfrac{35\pi}{6}+6\pi=\tfrac{\pi}6−635π​+6π=6π​. So the power is 128eiπ/6=643+64i128\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/6}=\boxed{64\sqrt3+64\mathrm{i}}128eiπ/6=643​+64i​.

(b) 1−3 i=2e−iπ/31-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i}=2\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi/3}1−3​i=2e−iπ/3, so (1−3 i)−5=2−5ei5π/3=132e−iπ/3=132(12−32i)=164−364 i.(1-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i})^{-5}=2^{-5}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}5\pi/3}=\tfrac1{32}\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi/3} =\tfrac1{32}\Bigl(\tfrac12-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\mathrm{i}\Bigr) =\boxed{\tfrac1{64}-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{64}\,\mathrm{i}}.(1−3​i)−5=2−5ei5π/3=321​e−iπ/3=321​(21​−23​​i)=641​−643​​i​.

Check. Multiply out a low power. (−3−i)3=−8i(-\sqrt3-\mathrm{i})^3=-8\mathrm{i}(−3​−i)3=−8i, so (−3−i)7=(−8i)2(−3−i)=643+64i(-\sqrt3-\mathrm{i})^7=(-8\mathrm{i})^2(-\sqrt3-\mathrm{i})=64\sqrt3+64\mathrm{i}(−3​−i)7=(−8i)2(−3​−i)=643​+64i. And (1−3 i)3=−8(1-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i})^3=-8(1−3​i)3=−8, so (1−3 i)−5=(1−3 i)/(1−3 i)6=164(1−3 i)(1-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i})^{-5}=(1-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i})/(1-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i})^6=\tfrac1{64}(1-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i})(1−3​i)−5=(1−3​i)/(1−3​i)6=641​(1−3​i).

Pitfalls

  • Raising the modulus but not multiplying the argument, or the reverse.

  • Expanding by the binomial theorem: it gives the same answer in eight terms instead of one line.

  • Losing track of the turns: −35π6-\tfrac{35\pi}6−635π​ is π6\tfrac{\pi}66π​ less three whole turns, not −5π6-\tfrac{5\pi}6−65π​ less some.

3.3 nnnth roots, and the roots of unity

Problem. Find every www with wn=zw^n=zwn=z, in exponential or Cartesian form.

Method

  1. Write z=reiθz=r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}z=reiθ, with the quadrant checked. (If z=0z=0z=0, the only root is w=0w=0w=0.)

  2. The roots all have modulus ρ=r1/n\rho=r^{1/n}ρ=r1/n, the positive real root.

  3. Their arguments are ϕk=θ+2πkn\phi_k=\dfrac{\theta+2\pi k}{n}ϕk​=nθ+2πk​ for k=0,1,…,n−1k=0,1,\dots,n-1k=0,1,…,n−1: exactly nnn of them.

  4. Write wk=ρ eiϕkw_k=\rho\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\phi_k}wk​=ρeiϕk​, and convert to Cartesian form if asked. Each root is the previous one turned through 2πn\tfrac{2\pi}nn2π​: wk=w0 e2πik/nw_k=w_0\,\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}k/n}wk​=w0​e2πik/n.

  5. The roots are the corners of a regular nnn-gon on the circle of radius ρ\rhoρ.

Variants. The roots of unity are the case z=1z=1z=1: the powers of ω=e2πi/n\omega=\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}/n}ω=e2πi/n, which add up to 000 for n≥2n\ge2n≥2. A square root of zzz when arg⁡z\arg zargz is not a standard angle: put (a+bi)2=z(a+b\mathrm{i})^2=z(a+bi)2=z, equate the parts, and add a2+b2=∣z∣a^2+b^2=\left|z\right|a2+b2=∣z∣ from the moduli. Solve for a2a^2a2 and b2b^2b2, and choose the signs so that 2ab=Imz2ab=\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}z2ab=Imz: the roots are ±(a+bi)\pm(a+b\mathrm{i})±(a+bi). An equation such as zn=c z‾z^n=c\,\overline{z}zn=cz: treat z=0z=0z=0 separately, then match the moduli and the arguments.

Example Solve w4=−8+83 iw^4=-8+8\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i}w4=−8+83​i in Cartesian form.

∣z∣=64+192=16\left|z\right|=\sqrt{64+192}=16∣z∣=64+192​=16, and zzz is in the second quadrant with reference angle arctan⁡3=π3\arctan\sqrt3=\tfrac\pi3arctan3​=3π​, so θ=2π3\theta=\tfrac{2\pi}3θ=32π​. Then ρ=161/4=2\rho=16^{1/4}=2ρ=161/4=2 and ϕk=2π/3+2πk4=π6+kπ2,k=0,1,2,3:π6, 2π3, 7π6, 5π3.\phi_k=\frac{2\pi/3+2\pi k}{4}=\frac\pi6+\frac{k\pi}2,\qquad\allowbreak k=0,1,2,3:\quad\allowbreak \tfrac\pi6,\ \tfrac{2\pi}3,\ \tfrac{7\pi}6,\ \tfrac{5\pi}3 .ϕk​=42π/3+2πk​=6π​+2kπ​,k=0,1,2,3:6π​, 32π​, 67π​, 35π​. The roots, the corners of a square on the circle of radius 222, are 3+i,  −1+3 i,  −3−i,  1−3 i\boxed{\sqrt3+\mathrm{i},\ \ -1+\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i},\ \ -\sqrt3-\mathrm{i},\ \ 1-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i}}3​+i,  −1+3​i,  −3​−i,  1−3​i​

Check. Raise one root to the fourth power: (3+i)4=(2eiπ/6)4=16ei2π/3=−8+83 i(\sqrt3+\mathrm{i})^4=(2\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/6})^4=16\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}2\pi/3}=-8+8\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i}(3​+i)4=(2eiπ/6)4=16ei2π/3=−8+83​i. The four roots add up to 000, as the corners of a regular polygon centred at 000 must.

Pitfalls

  • Forgetting the 2πk2\pi k2πk: it gives one root instead of nnn.

  • Running kkk up to nnn: k=nk=nk=n repeats the root for k=0k=0k=0.

  • Taking ρ=r\rho=rρ=r instead of r1/nr^{1/n}r1/n.

3.4 Identities from De Moivre and the inverse Euler formulas

Problem. Write cos⁡nθ\cos n\thetacosnθ or sin⁡nθ\sin n\thetasinnθ in powers of cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ and sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ; write a power of cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ or sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ as a sum of multiple angles; evaluate a trigonometric or hyperbolic function at an imaginary number.

Method

  1. Multiple angle: expand (cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)n(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^n(cosθ+isinθ)n by the binomial theorem. By De Moivre it equals cos⁡nθ+isin⁡nθ\cos n\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin n\thetacosnθ+isinnθ. Compare the real parts and the imaginary parts. Use sin⁡2θ=1−cos⁡2θ\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\thetasin2θ=1−cos2θ if one function is asked for.

  2. Power: substitute cos⁡θ=12(eiθ+e−iθ)\cos\theta=\tfrac12(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}+\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta})cosθ=21​(eiθ+e−iθ) or sin⁡θ=12i(eiθ−e−iθ)\sin\theta=\tfrac1{2\mathrm{i}}(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}-\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta})sinθ=2i1​(eiθ−e−iθ), take the factor (12)n(\tfrac12)^n(21​)n or (12i)n(\tfrac1{2\mathrm{i}})^n(2i1​)n outside, and expand.

  3. Pair each eikθ\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k\theta}eikθ with e−ikθ\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}k\theta}e−ikθ: their sum is 2cos⁡kθ2\cos k\theta2coskθ, their difference 2isin⁡kθ2\mathrm{i}\sin k\theta2isinkθ. Simplify.

  4. Imaginary argument: put ix\mathrm{i}xix into the inverse Euler formula, use i2=−1\mathrm{i}^2=-1i2=−1, and recognise cosh⁡x\cosh xcoshx or sinh⁡x\sinh xsinhx. So cos⁡(ix)=cosh⁡x\cos(\mathrm{i}x)=\cosh xcos(ix)=coshx and sin⁡(ix)=isinh⁡x\sin(\mathrm{i}x)=\mathrm{i}\sinh xsin(ix)=isinhx. Putting ix\mathrm{i}xix into cosh⁡z=12(ez+e−z)\cosh z=\tfrac12(\mathrm{e}^z+\mathrm{e}^{-z})coshz=21​(ez+e−z) and sinh⁡z=12(ez−e−z)\sinh z=\tfrac12(\mathrm{e}^z-\mathrm{e}^{-z})sinhz=21​(ez−e−z) gives cosh⁡(ix)=cos⁡x\cosh(\mathrm{i}x)=\cos xcosh(ix)=cosx and sinh⁡(ix)=isin⁡x\sinh(\mathrm{i}x)=\mathrm{i}\sin xsinh(ix)=isinx.

Example (a) Write sin⁡5θ\sin5\thetasin5θ in powers of s=sin⁡θs=\sin\thetas=sinθ. (b) Write cos⁡3θ\cos^3\thetacos3θ as a sum of cosines of multiples of θ\thetaθ. (c) Evaluate sin⁡(iln⁡3)\sin(\mathrm{i}\ln 3)sin(iln3).

(a) With c=cos⁡θc=\cos\thetac=cosθ, the imaginary terms of (c+is)5(c+\mathrm{i}s)^5(c+is)5 are 5c4(is)+10c2(is)3+(is)5=i(5c4s−10c2s3+s5)5c^4(\mathrm{i}s)+10c^2(\mathrm{i}s)^3+(\mathrm{i}s)^5=\mathrm{i}(5c^4s-10c^2s^3+s^5)5c4(is)+10c2(is)3+(is)5=i(5c4s−10c2s3+s5). Comparing imaginary parts with cos⁡5θ+isin⁡5θ\cos5\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin5\thetacos5θ+isin5θ, and using c2=1−s2c^2=1-s^2c2=1−s2, sin⁡5θ=5(1−s2)2s−10(1−s2)s3+s5=16s5−20s3+5s.\begin{align*} \sin5\theta&=5(1-s^2)^2s-10(1-s^2)s^3+s^5\\ &=\boxed{16s^5-20s^3+5s}. \end{align*}sin5θ​=5(1−s2)2s−10(1−s2)s3+s5=16s5−20s3+5s​.​ (b) Put u=eiθu=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}u=eiθ. Then cos⁡3θ=18(u+u−1)3=18(u3+u−3+3(u+u−1))=18(2cos⁡3θ+6cos⁡θ)=14cos⁡3θ+34cos⁡θ.\cos^3\theta=\tfrac18\bigl(u+u^{-1}\bigr)^3=\tfrac18\bigl(u^3+u^{-3}+3(u+u^{-1})\bigr) =\tfrac18\bigl(2\cos3\theta+6\cos\theta\bigr) =\boxed{\tfrac14\cos3\theta+\tfrac34\cos\theta}.cos3θ=81​(u+u−1)3=81​(u3+u−3+3(u+u−1))=81​(2cos3θ+6cosθ)=41​cos3θ+43​cosθ​. (c) sin⁡(iln⁡3)=isinh⁡(ln⁡3)=i⋅12(3−13)=43 i\sin(\mathrm{i}\ln3)=\mathrm{i}\sinh(\ln3)=\mathrm{i}\cdot\tfrac12\bigl(3-\tfrac13\bigr)=\boxed{\tfrac43\,\mathrm{i}}sin(iln3)=isinh(ln3)=i⋅21​(3−31​)=34​i​.

Check. Test at an angle where nothing vanishes. At θ=π6\theta=\tfrac\pi6θ=6π​, where s=12s=\tfrac12s=21​: sin⁡5π6=12=1632−208+52\sin\tfrac{5\pi}6=\tfrac12=\tfrac{16}{32}-\tfrac{20}8+\tfrac52sin65π​=21​=3216​−820​+25​. At θ=π3\theta=\tfrac\pi3θ=3π​: cos⁡3π3=18=14(−1)+34⋅12\cos^3\tfrac\pi3=\tfrac18=\tfrac14(-1)+\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac12cos33π​=81​=41​(−1)+43​⋅21​. For (c), from the inverse Euler formula directly: sin⁡(iln⁡3)=12i(e−ln⁡3−eln⁡3)=12i(13−3)=43i\sin(\mathrm{i}\ln3)=\tfrac1{2\mathrm{i}}(\mathrm{e}^{-\ln3}-\mathrm{e}^{\ln3})=\tfrac1{2\mathrm{i}}(\tfrac13-3)=\tfrac43\mathrm{i}sin(iln3)=2i1​(e−ln3−eln3)=2i1​(31​−3)=34​i.

Pitfalls

  • Getting (2i)n(2\mathrm{i})^n(2i)n wrong: (2i)2=−4(2\mathrm{i})^2=-4(2i)2=−4 and (2i)3=−8i(2\mathrm{i})^3=-8\mathrm{i}(2i)3=−8i.

  • Comparing parts before the expansion is complete, or putting a term with i2\mathrm{i}^2i2 in the imaginary part.

  • Writing cos⁡(ix)=icosh⁡x\cos(\mathrm{i}x)=\mathrm{i}\cosh xcos(ix)=icoshx. The cosine of an imaginary number is real: cos⁡(ix)=cosh⁡x\cos(\mathrm{i}x)=\cosh xcos(ix)=coshx.

3.5 Adding sinusoids with phasors

Problem. Write a sum of sinusoids of one angular frequency ω\omegaω (not the root of unity of Method 3.3) as a single sinusoid Rcos⁡(ωt+α)R\cos(\omega t+\alpha)Rcos(ωt+α).

Method

  1. Write every term as Acos⁡(ωt+φ)A\cos(\omega t+\varphi)Acos(ωt+φ) with A>0A>0A>0. A sine becomes a cosine by sin⁡x=cos⁡(x−π2)\sin x=\cos(x-\tfrac\pi2)sinx=cos(x−2π​), and a minus sign by −cos⁡x=cos⁡(x+π)-\cos x=\cos(x+\pi)−cosx=cos(x+π).

  2. Each term’s phasor is P=AeiφP=A\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}P=Aeiφ.

  3. Add the phasors in Cartesian form. If they add up to 000, the signal is identically 000 and has no phase.

  4. Otherwise find the modulus RRR and the argument α\alphaα of the sum, quadrant first.

  5. The sum is Rcos⁡(ωt+α)R\cos(\omega t+\alpha)Rcos(ωt+α). If the question asks for Rcos⁡(ωt−β)R\cos(\omega t-\beta)Rcos(ωt−β), then β=−α\beta=-\alphaβ=−α.

Example Write 4cos⁡(ωt+5π6)−4sin⁡ωt4\cos(\omega t+\tfrac{5\pi}6)-4\sin\omega t4cos(ωt+65π​)−4sinωt as a single sinusoid.

By both rules of step 1, −sin⁡x=−cos⁡(x−π2)=cos⁡(x+π2)-\sin x=-\cos(x-\tfrac\pi2)=\cos(x+\tfrac\pi2)−sinx=−cos(x−2π​)=cos(x+2π​), so the phasors are P1=4ei5π/6=−23+2iP_1=4\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}5\pi/6}=-2\sqrt3+2\mathrm{i}P1​=4ei5π/6=−23​+2i and P2=4eiπ/2=4iP_2=4\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/2}=4\mathrm{i}P2​=4eiπ/2=4i. Their sum is −23+6i-2\sqrt3+6\mathrm{i}−23​+6i, in the second quadrant, with reference angle arctan⁡623=arctan⁡3=π3\arctan\tfrac{6}{2\sqrt3}=\arctan\sqrt3=\tfrac\pi3arctan23​6​=arctan3​=3π​. So R=12+36=43,α=π−π3=2π3,R=\sqrt{12+36}=4\sqrt3,\qquad\allowbreak \alpha=\pi-\tfrac\pi3=\tfrac{2\pi}{3},R=12+36​=43​,α=π−3π​=32π​, and the sum is 43cos⁡(ωt+2π3)\boxed{4\sqrt3\cos\bigl(\omega t+\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\bigr)}43​cos(ωt+32π​)​, with amplitude about 6.936.936.93.

Check. At ωt=0\omega t=0ωt=0: 4cos⁡5π6=−23=43cos⁡2π34\cos\tfrac{5\pi}6=-2\sqrt3=4\sqrt3\cos\tfrac{2\pi}34cos65π​=−23​=43​cos32π​. At ωt=π2\omega t=\tfrac\pi2ωt=2π​, where the sine term counts in full: 4cos⁡4π3−4=−6=43cos⁡7π64\cos\tfrac{4\pi}3-4=-6=4\sqrt3\cos\tfrac{7\pi}64cos34π​−4=−6=43​cos67π​.

Pitfalls

  • Adding the amplitudes: 4+4=84+4=84+4=8 is too big unless the phases agree.

  • Turning a sine the wrong way: sin⁡x=cos⁡(x−π2)\sin x=\cos(x-\tfrac\pi2)sinx=cos(x−2π​), not cos⁡(x+π2)\cos(x+\tfrac\pi2)cos(x+2π​).

  • Reading α\alphaα off arctan⁡\arctanarctan when the phasor sum is in the second or third quadrant: here arctan⁡6−23=−π3\arctan\tfrac{6}{-2\sqrt3}=-\tfrac\pi3arctan−23​6​=−3π​ points the wrong way.

In the notes. Unit 3: Application: phasors and AC analysis.
